title: Seeds
hook: the first order covers blessings and farming

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shas, and your line: six orders. Zeraim, Moed, Nashim, Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot. Can you still say them? Today, we walk into the first one. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

A farmer walks out at dawn to a field of wheat that's ready. Before a single stalk is cut, a whole list of questions is waiting for her. Which edge of the field stays standing? What happens to the stalks she drops? Did she plant two kinds of seed in one row? Is this the year the land is supposed to rest? Which part of the harvest goes to someone else? On a grocery receipt, a harvest looks simple: grow it, cut it, sell it, eat it. The Mishnah's first order looks at that same field and sees a web of obligations. It's named for what goes into the ground.
screen: `A FIELD AT DAWN, READY TO CUT.` → `A LIST OF QUESTIONS WAITING.` → `NAMED FOR WHAT GOES IN THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Zeraim. Seeds. The first of the six orders. It opens with blessings, which is tomorrow's story, and then it goes out to the farm and stays there. Walk through a growing season with it. Before planting, there's Kilayim, mixed kinds. The Torah says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt not sow thy field with two kinds of seed." So the Mishnah asks the practical questions: how far apart do two crops have to be? What counts as two kinds? Then there's Sheviit, the seventh year. The Torah tells the farmer to let the land rest, and says the poor may eat what grows on its own. Then the harvest itself, and here the gifts begin. Peah, the corner of the field, left for the poor. Terumot and Maaserot, the portions set aside for the priests and the Levites, who had no fields of their own. And at the end of the order, Bikkurim, the first fruits brought up to the Temple. Notice the pattern. At every stage of the year, the harvest is never only the farmer's. Something goes to the poor. Something goes to the priest and the Levite. Something goes to the land itself, which gets its rest. And something goes back to God. Jewish law ties these farm laws largely to the land of Israel, so a Jewish farmer in Ohio isn't bound by most of them. But the order still says something to anyone who eats: food arrives already carrying other people's shares.
screen: `ZERAIM: THE FIRST ORDER, SEEDS.` · `MIXED KINDS AND THE SEVENTH YEAR.` · `THE CORNER, THE TITHES, FIRST FRUITS.` · `A HARVEST IS NEVER ONLY YOURS.` · then, large: `SEEDS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: bless one food. Take something small you're about to eat: an apple, a piece of bread, a handful of nuts. Hold it, and sit with it through the bell. Trace it backward. Who picked it, packed it, drove it? What field or orchard did it come from? What rain fell on it? Then, before you eat, if you pray, you can say the blessing your tradition uses for that food. If you don't, name out loud where it grew and one person who helped it reach you. The bell holds the time.
Zeraim. Seeds: the first order of the Mishnah, on blessings and farming, where every harvest carries shares for others. Today's word.
Your line: seeds. Today, at one meal, notice who else has a share in what's on your plate. Tomorrow, why a book about farming opens with blessings. Day one thousand sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating, with different endings for bread, fruit of the tree, fruit of the ground and other foods; in the land of Israel, farmers who keep these laws still set aside tithes and observe the seventh year.
